https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820: Watch: Zelensky questions "strange'" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckm2: Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.

More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. More than 400 flights in the US were cancelled on Thursday and another 2,200 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.
The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.
Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.
FedEx aircraft sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly: A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.
Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.
Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.
Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.
A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled)
At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.
There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.
In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."
French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.
The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.
While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".
Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.
In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.
In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.
Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.
News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.
He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk: The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning.
Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline . It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly: Gérard Depardieu has faced a series of allegations in recent years on film sets and elsewhere
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc ( call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9m2: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.

The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w: A Rheinmetall facility in Kuwait was targeted by Iran, Italian and Kuwaiti authorities said
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.
Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.

Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region.
"The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members.
"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added.
"Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them.
"Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives."
Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.
The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3gr: Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.

The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".

"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."

At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.

A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly: Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering new hope for HIV prevention?
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025 .
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c61w: Myanmar's president Min Aung Hlaing has led the country since he seized power in a 2021 military coup

Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.
The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.
The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.
The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.
The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.
But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.
While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.
More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders .

Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3: Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.
Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.
Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".
"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."
Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023
Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".
Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."
In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".
US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".
Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".
Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982

Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."

She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".
Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/world/2809117: The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating an incident at Sydney Airport involving Qantas and Air New Zealand aircraft.
Qantas flight QF426 from Melbourne abandoned its landing approach after crew in the cockpit saw an Air New Zealand aircraft crossing the runway.
The incident happened at 10.15am local time on Wednesday morning and involved a Qantas Boeing 737 and an Air New Zealand Airbus A321.
In a statement, the ATSB said air traffic controllers had advised the Qantas flight crew to expect a late landing clearance due to aircraft crossing the runway.

"As the 737 continued the approach, and prior to receiving a clearance to land, the crew reported seeing an Air New Zealand A321 crossing the runway at taxiway Golf. The crew of the 737 elected to conduct a go-around.

"The evidence collection phase of the investigation will involve interviewing involved flight crew and air traffic controllers, retrieving and reviewing available recorded data such as air traffic control audio, movement guidance and control system recordings and any available CCTV, and the collection of other relevant information including manuals and procedures.
"In particular, the investigation will seek to ascertain what information was provided to the crews of both aircraft, and what mental models those crews held," the ATSB said in a statement.
Qantas has said it will support the ATSB as it conducts its investigation.
"Our pilots were following Air Traffic Control instructions and elected to conduct a go-around as the other aircraft was crossing the runway," a Qantas spokesperson told RNZ.

Earlier this year, a number of incidents occurring at Sydney Airport made headlines, including a near-collision in July that investigators described as one of the most severe runway conflicts on record.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/life/relationships: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/life/relationships/family%2Fthe-path-to-solo-motherhood-was-filled-with-fear-and-loss-but-i-ve-never-been-happier
For many years, Jane Biggin felt the pressure to find a partner before it was too late.
Jane Biggin desperately wanted children and says she was dating to "find a baby daddy" rather than a relationship.

"I was less focused on my attraction to the person and whether I wanted to have a relationship with him, and started to focus more on what's he going to be like as a dad, is this going to last, do I even bother?" says the 38-year-old midwife from Melbourne/Naarm.
Jane made a commitment to herself that if she hadn't met someone by 35, she would pursue motherhood solo.
Jane Biggin says she wanted to be a mum more than she wanted a relationship.
While many patients have their surplus embryos discarded by IVF clinics, some find themselves attached to the microscopic cell cluster.
As financial and time pressures seem to ever increase for parents, some are doubling down on growing their family, even if that means a vasectomy reversal.
“For the longest time, I was hoping and expecting it to happen organically and now it feels like intervention is required.”
"I knew in my bones that I needed to be a mum more than I needed to be in a relationship."
Jane is now mum to 16-month-old Jude. The road to meet him was filled with fear and loss, but she is now in a place she describes as "more amazing that I could ever have imagined".
In my teens I was into everything at school; drama, sport. I just wasn't that interested in dating.
Then in my 20s I was travelling and did a couple of university degrees.
I always felt like a relationship would be nice to have but not something I needed.
I did date in my 20s and 30s, but nothing every really eventuated. I feel dating is such a numbers game, and I probably didn't do it enough.
I would often get those stereotypical comments like "I don't understand why you are single" and "lower your standards".
There is this assumption if you are older and single it's because your expectations are too high.
I don't agree with that. And I don't think you should have to settle.
My early 30s was when I really started feeling the pressure to find someone.
I'm a midwife and have this hyper awareness of what the stats are around fertility. I'm also seeing people make families 24/7.
I knew that I really wanted to be a mum. And when dating with that, you are putting the pressure of an entire life with this person, rather than dating for the thrill and the connection.
It was in the back of my mind that if I make the wrong decision here, I could set myself back five years.
I had worked with a couple of solo mums by choice or people having babies with friends.
I was lucky enough to be exposed to people who were having these non-conventional families.
I basically had a deadline of 35 in my head; if I hit my 35th birthday and I'm still not in a relationship, I'm just going to do this.
The longer you wait the more likely you will potentially miss out, and some fertility testing suggested I should get started sooner rather than later.
My main fears were that if I go in this direction, I'm closing the door on the opportunity to have the good old-fashioned relationship I had envisioned.
My biggest fear was the financial side of it. I was a single income earner, and I knew I would have to do IVF, which is expensive.
It took five rounds of IVF and cost me AU$40,000. I used a donor through a clinic.
I was terrified about having twins because it was all my fears multiplied. Part financial, part knowing what can go wrong.
But I did get to a point that I was happy about it. I had wanted more than one child, and it meant I would never have to do IVF again.

Rylan Urquhart picked up the guitar as a kid thanks to the American star. Fourteen years later, he found himself on stage performing with his idol.
Dunedin singer and guitar player Rylan Urquhart’s dream was to open for American star Jack Johnson at his New Zealand shows.
So it was a surreal moment for the 21-year-old to be suddenly called up on stage while watching his idol perform last week in Auckland.
“I actually started playing [the guitar] because of Jack Johnson. My parents took me to one of his concerts when I was a kid… So it kind of makes this whole thing a little bit full circle.”
Rylan Urquhart with Jack Johnson on stage at the Christchurch show on 22 November, 2026.
Katie has always dreamed of having Robbie Williams sing for her. That dream came true on Tuesday night.
During interval at the Sydney orchestral performance the keyboard player suddenly fell ill. A local student stepped up to fill in with no notice.
"The electricity made it like you're not allowed. It's like, what do you mean I'm not allowed?"

Ahead of the show he hadn’t heard anything back about his audition to open for Johnson, apart from word circulating that “something could happen”. Still, he and his father and brother rocked up as superfans in the front row.
“There was this really interesting point in the show where Jack started playing one of his songs, and I sort of saw him catch my eye a little bit.
“I could have sworn he mouthed ‘Hi Rylan’. I was like, ‘what the heck? Surely that didn't happen, right?’ I was like, ‘there's no way that just happened. I don't think he knows who I am’.”
A couple of songs later, as Johnson took audience requests, he asked Urquhart to join him on stage.

“There was definitely this moment where I'm like, ‘what the heck? This is happening’ as I'm jumping over the barricade. I get up on stage. Jack gives me a hug. Then in that moment I just knew I kind of had to lock in a little bit… and just do my best to hopefully not sound like garbage in front of 13,000 people.”
Hearing the crowd’s support was one of the coolest experiences, he says.
And he got to relive it when he headed to the Christchurch show with more of his family members and mates.
Rylan Urquhart got a chance to perform on stage with American singer Jack Johnson in Christchurch on 22 November, 2026.
This time, he did get a five-minute warning before the show to “be on standby”. While there were some nerves in the build-up, he knew he could do it after the sudden call-up in Auckland.
“He was like, ‘I want to bring my new friend Rylan on stage’, which is crazy."

“While I was up there, Jack, he kind of talked a little bit about that last show, and he actually said he'd listen to some of my own original music and just said some really kind words about that as well, which was just really sweet of him, to be honest. He's like a really nice guy.
“Just hearing that was a little bit surreal, but I was just so, so thankful to hear someone whose music that I respect so much speak about my own in that way.
“So a really, really special moment for me that I'll never forget.”

Urquhart’s music journey and influence start from a young age. From his country musician great-grandma and piano-playing grandma to his guitar-playing nana, who would drag him to country music club, and trumpet-playing father, there’s no shortage of talent in the family.
At school, Urquhart took part in talent shows and the Smokefreerockquest, and eventually won The Hits’ Kid Sheeran contest, where the then-13-year-old got to meet Ed Sheeran in person.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6r7: There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.
US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC , external : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."
The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.
It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20: The UK has agreed the deals in a bit to cut red tape for British companies
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.
The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.
It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.
Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.
Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.
The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.
This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.
But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.
However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".
It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.
The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.
The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.
But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.
But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqev: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.
Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.
From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.
In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.
That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.
For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.
It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.
That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.
"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".
Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.
On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.
Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.
"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.
But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: Self-confessed foodie Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats is "empowering"
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat - bliss.
"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.
The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.
As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."
We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.
Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.
She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.
"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.
"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."
Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".
"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."
While solo dining Catherine likes to read, journal or simply enjoy the peace and quiet

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.
Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.
Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.
"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.
"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."
A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.
"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.
Ruth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be alone

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".
But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.
"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."
SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg5: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.
That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.
Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.
On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.
Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.
However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

She is far from alone, with one million homeowners facing a similar increase often because they are coming off deals that were agreed before interest rates began rising in 2022.
The Bank's report said that households facing higher payments "may need to reduce discretionary spending or draw down savings as higher energy and other essential costs feed through".
Most had savings buffers but lower-income households, including renters, had less wriggle room owing to spending a greater proportion of their income on essentials.

The numbers could change were mortgage rates to fall, primarily if international economic volatility eased.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62k: The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.
They point to improving sales over recent months as proof the business had a future.
MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".
No-one appears to dispute the fact that Gordon Brothers' insistence that they get paid most of their £22.5m debt was a major stumbling block to a sale.
Potential buyers balked at paying out millions on a loan that Gordon Brothers inherited for nothing.

Martin Property Group offered £5m up front with the balance to be deferred, while Xyra Holdings offered £12.5m up front but, according to sources close to the deal, were thought unable to actually pay.
Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised.
First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year.
The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme.
Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates.
In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it.
Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth.
It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely.

Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup."
Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff.
But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed.
Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them.
In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees.

Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c52e: Jim Lembesis has been working on elevators in Chicago for 47 years
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.
"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."
Lift and escalator technicians "amaze" with their ability to fix things
Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped , external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.
In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic , external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."
Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.
"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."
In the US there's a four-year apprenticeship to become a lift technician

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.
"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.
But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.
