https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: The Springboks and All Blacks played three Tests in South Africa before a fourth in the American city of Baltimore
South Africa and New Zealand players were not subjected to a single post-match drugs test by anti-doping authorities when they contested this year's Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
The four-Test series, played in August and September, is a new biennial initiative between the two southern hemisphere powerhouses aimed at boosted revenues and profiles.
An agreement over how the series operates refers to World Rugby anti-doping rules; but, in practice, post-match tests, which are standard practice at most elite-level matches, were not carried out.
Players in the series could have been tested by either of two official bodies.
All players involved in the series are part of World Rugby's testing pool. The global governing body conducts on-the-spot tests on top players around the world throughout the year.
The South African Institute for Drug-Free Sport (Saids) runs its own domestic anti-doping programme, covering sporting events and athletes in the country.
With all matches, bar the fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore, taking place in South Africa, Saids could have demanded samples from players after games.
World Rugby would not confirm the lack of post-match testing in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, but it stressed that all players are subject to the "always-on" testing regime.
"World Rugby operates a risk-based no-notice anti-doping programme in line with the World Anti-Doping Agency code," said a spokesperson.
"All qualified men's and women's Rugby World Cup team players are included within a dedicated out-of-competition testing pool which is not competition specific.
"This means that all these players are subject to testing on a no-notice, any location basis throughout the calendar year, including within international competition windows.

"This means that over the course of the year, both teams are tested in and out of competition in line with World Rugby's programme and are also subject to testing undertaken by the respective national anti-doping agencies at both the international and domestic/cross border club levels."
Saids referred queries about testing in Rugby's Greatest Rivalry back to World Rugby, saying the global body had "jurisdiction" over the matches.
The latest figures from the World Anti-Doping Agency show there were 9,583 accredited doping tests in rugby union globally in 2024, with 0.6% coming back positive.
That number of tests is fewer than those conducted in athletics (44,044), cycling (26,156), aquatics (17,447), but more than in wrestling (7,620), triathlon, (4,478) and gymnastics (4,190).
The number of rugby players tested by Saids has fallen significantly in recent years.
The most recent Saids annual report, covering the 12 months to 31 March, records 225 tests in the sport.
UK Anti-Doping, which covers England, Scotland and Wales, carried out 1,086 tests in rugby union in 2025. New Zealand's Sport Integrity Commission conducted 249 tests in rugby over the same period.
Currently two rugby union players in New Zealand – both well below elite level – are serving suspensions for doping.
The cost of testing has dramatically increased for Saids after the World Anti-Doping Agency revoked its accreditation for a sample-testing laboratory in Bloemfontein in May 2025. , external

With no other such facilities in Africa, Saids has to send samples long distances for testing. It says its budget has been hit by foreign currency costs from overseas laboratories, courier costs and import charges.
While elsewhere violations have mainly been restricted to players outside the elite, the Springboks have been hit by several doping cases in recent years.

Great Britain advanced to the semi-finals of the Davis Cup for the first time since 2019 as Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won a decisive doubles tie against third seeds Germany in Bologna.
Patten and Skupski, playing together for the first time since announcing their doubles partnership for the 2027 season, proved too clinical for Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz.
They converted two break points and saved five in the first set, before overturning a mini-break in the tie-break to win 6-2 7-6 (8-6).

Skupski was involved in a Davis Cup quarter-final loss playing alongside Joe Salisbury against the same German doubles pair in December 2021 - a defeat that was in his mind as Thursday's decider progressed.
"I thought about that match during the match today and I was determined not to let that happen again," Skupski told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"No matter what was happening today, we weren't going to come off the court very easily with a loss."

World number one Alexander Zverev had earlier sent the tie to its full distance by defeating British number one Arthur Fery in straight sets to cancel out Cameron Norrie's three-set victory over Jan-Lennard Struff.
Great Britain's semi-final is scheduled for Saturday, when they will face Spain.
Spaniards Daniel Merida and Rafael Jodar won their singles matches, meaning the team did not need to play doubles, allowing Carlos Alcaraz to rest.
Captain David Ferrer said Alcaraz may be in contention to play in the singles against Great Britain.
Defending champions Italy will play the Czech Republic in Friday's first semi-final.
Recap: GB's Davis Cup quarter-final win against Germany as it happened

Smith will step down as captain at the end of the tournament and Great Britain retain hopes of a second victory under his leadership, following the most recent of their 10 Davis Cup successes in 2015.
"I felt the same sort of pressure, nerves and butterflies beforehand and during the matches," said Smith, who has been captain since 2010.

"You sit for a long time in that chair on your own on a day like this, a lot of thoughts go through your head and one of the things I kept reminding myself is how much of a privilege it is to be in this situation.

"I loved it but, more importantly, I'm thrilled for the guys. They've committed so well to this, they've been to a few different places over the past 18 months to get to this opportunity and I'm delighted they've got to the final four now."
Highlights: Norrie beats Struff in three sets to give GB lead in Davis Cup
World number 52 Norrie had got Great Britain off to the perfect start with a three-set win against Struff, a player 13 places above him in the world rankings.
The left-hander raced through the first set in just 23 minutes but a break late in the second set by Struff forced a decider.
The key moment came at 2-2 in the final set when Norrie saved four break points to hold serve, after which he won 12 of the next 14 points to complete a 6-3 3-6 6-2 victory.
Norrie's success meant a win for Fery against Zverev, a two-time major champion in 2026, would have been enough to secure Great Britain's passage through to the last four.
However, as he did in their Wimbledon semi-final in July, Zverev proved too strong for 24-year-old Fery and ended as a 6-3 6-2 winner.

Germany international Laura Freigang has been suspended from football for 16 months over issues with three drugs tests.
The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 October 2027.
The 16-month suspension begins from the date of notification by the German Football Association (DFB), which took place in June.
The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the National Anti-Doping Agency (Nada), DFB and Freigang reached a dispute resolution agreement.
The dispute said Entracht Frankfurt forward Freigang committed three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026.
Freigang can return to training two months prior to the end of the suspension period but cannot play matches until after 7 October.
All personal records of appearances, goals, assists or other statistics from 23 February 2026 are nullified, though Frankfurt's results are unaffected.
This season Freigang has scored six goals and provided two assists in 11 starts in the Frauen-Bundesliga.
Since joining the club in 2020, the striker has scored 107 goals in 187 appearances and was in the Germany squad for October's friendly victories over Australia and Japan.
In a club statement , external , Franfurt said they will "begin discussions shortly to determine the terms of her future employment relationship".
Freigang's current contract is due to expire on 30 June 2027.

Frankfurt's director of women's football Katharina Kiel said: "The agreement now reached provides clarity and planning security in a process unprecedented for Eintracht Frankfurt - for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

"The way she and the team have handled the situation in recent months, and how Laura personally led by example with her performance on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the highest recognition.
"The identified shortcomings, despite the agreement to settle the dispute, have resulted in a suspension, which means the loss of a key player."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Nigel Starmer-Smith voiced BBC's rugby union highlights show, Rugby Special
Former England scrum-half and rugby union commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith has died aged 81.
Starmer-Smith represented Harlequins and the Barbarians, and made seven appearances for England between 1969-71.
After his retirement in 1976, Starmer-Smith moved into broadcasting and journalism.
He voiced the BBC's highlights programme Rugby Special for 15 years and commentated for ITV at the 2003 World Cup in Australia, won by England.

Starmer-Smith's son Charlie spoke about his father's condition in 2021, saying dementia was a "big issue" in sport and describing how the family were only able to see him through the window during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He said that getting knocked out in a game of rugby was "like a badge of honour" during his father's playing days but also said dementia ran in their family, with his uncle also dying from the disease.
"Dad passed away peacefully this morning after a long battle with dementia," Charlie posted on social media on Thursday.

"He was (as they say in rugby circles) one of life's great tourists. A rugby player, commentator, editor, writer, raconteur, charity fundraiser, volunteer, speaker, prankster, family man, life and soul of the party, but, above all, the greatest father anyone could wish to have.

"Just as I choose not to let the cruel condition that robbed him of his ability to communicate (and ultimately of his dignity), define my memories of him.

"He was a modest man and he'd hate for people to make a fuss. He loved to laugh but not as much as he loved to see others laughing. So for those that knew him think of a happy memory and smile. For that's how I'll remember him."

Alejandro Garnacho's time at Aston Villa has been brief - and it already looks to be over.
The latest snub by Villa boss Unai Emery was the most damming of all, with the on-loan Chelsea winger left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.
"The players who were here I think are the best players to be here with us," said Emery.
Villa could have had 12 substitutes in Istanbul but Emery chose just 11 - including two goalkeepers - as Garnacho stayed at home.
The plan was for the Argentina international's loan move to become permanent for £43m should certain criteria be met.
They are believed to be based on a number of appearances staff felt were so achievable the club were in little doubt he would become a Villa player.
Garnacho trained with Villa's first team on Monday but did not travel to Istanbul
"First start after three months. Happy to be enjoying football again."
The post Garnacho wrote on social media after a pre-season game in July has - along with anything else related to Villa - been deleted from his account.
He has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season, and seven of Villa's 11 games ended without him getting on the pitch.
His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.
Including Saturday's 0-0 draw with Sunderland , Garnacho has been omitted from the past three matchday squads - a strong sign Emery has lost faith in him.
But he may have been fighting a losing battle from the off, having arrived at Villa unfit.
Sources have acknowledged the 22-year-old was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.
He initially trained on his own, and questions over the signing were already being asked, with eyebrows raised by some internally given his inconsistent form for both Chelsea and Manchester United .
Yet he had been on Villa's list of targets - albeit a long list - while he was at Stamford Bridge as Emery was keen to sign a pacy winger in the summer.

Garnacho's problems were compounded by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season, and even a boot camp during the international break in September and October, and scoring in friendlies against Sevilla and Southampton have not helped.
One of the issues Villa have is there is no exit clause, and both teams would have to agree to end the season-long loan deal early.
This time last year, Emery had already decided not to sign Harvey Elliott permanently in a £30m deal , leaving the on-loan Liverpool midfielder in limbo for the rest of the season.
And it appears Emery has already come to the same conclusion with Garnacho.

With Villa unable to find a solution with Liverpool , Elliott wasted a precious year of his career. Those close to him recognise the damage last season did, playing just nine times after being named Player of the Tournament at the European Under-21 Championship in 2025.
He is now at Valencia and is yet to start in La Liga this season.

The risk of going on loan to Villa became a topic of conversation in the game because of Elliott's plight, with sources suggesting players would think twice about joining the club. Garnacho's situation only increases those concerns.
Three times in two seasons, Emery and Villa have signed a high-profile player on loan only for it to fail.

Jadon Sancho's expensive loan from Manchester United last season - Villa paying a guaranteed 80% of Sancho's wages of more than £200,000 a week - ended with him having made just nine Premier League starts and scoring once in 39 appearances, with 21 of those as a substitute.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/golf/article: Sir Nick Faldo has suggested , external those who financially benefited from LIV Golf should "chip in and take care of" businesses owed money by the Saudi-backed tour.
His comments have been welcomed by UK companies still waiting to be paid.
A BBC Sport investigation found that LIV paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while bills from suppliers were already overdue.
Faldo - arguably Britain's greatest golfer - said the controversial breakaway tour risked "ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible".
"British suppliers who cleaned venues and kept events running are still owed hundreds of thousands of pounds," added the six-time major winner.
"Maybe if those on and off the golf course feel they were overcompensated for their worth, they should chip in and take care of this matter."
Since the investigation was published, more firms have contacted us about money they are owed by LIV.
They include sports communications company Soapbox, which works with the likes of Anthony Joshua and Luke Littler and is owed tens of thousands of pounds.
"I'm incredibly grateful to Sir Nick Faldo for speaking out," said Krissi Foskett, whose cleaning company BD365 Clean is £75,225 out of pocket.
"For the last couple of months I've felt powerless. Having someone of his standing recognise the injustice of what's happening to businesses like ours genuinely means a lot.
"Sir Nick's suggestion that those who have benefited financially could contribute towards paying the outstanding suppliers is something I wholeheartedly welcome."
LIV Golf has not responded to requests for comment on the original investigation or Faldo's remarks.
In August, chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped the tour would be able to pay its suppliers.
"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed.
"I come from a family of entrepreneurs, a family of small business entrepreneurs and know the challenge."
Scott O'Neil (right) took over from Greg Norman (left) as LIV chief executive in January 2025
Faldo's one-time on-course rival, Greg Norman, was chief executive of LIV Golf until last year.
Court filings show the Australian received $9.4m (£7.2m) in settlement and bonus payments in September 2025.
His successor, O'Neil, received a retention bonus of $6.4m (£4.9m) in June this year.
In September, Norman told The Real Deal with Bob Philion podcast that he was proud of bringing private equity into the sport.
"In a period of basically 2021 to now, close to $8bn (£6.1bn) has been brought into the game of golf," he said.
Responding to those comments, Faldo told BBC Sport: "Eight billion dollars is 8,000 million dollars. If that is a full six years, that is approximately $3.6m (£2.8m) a day.
"Before LIV filed for bankruptcy, seven executives received $15.6m (£11.9m) in retention payments, with further bonuses also paid.
"Now they risk ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible."
Companies still owed money include Global Infusion Group, which provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event and is awaiting £321,671 - which was due on 7 August.
Public records also list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.
Just $2m (£1.5m) has been proposed so far by LIV's Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure whether they will receive anything at all.
"I've spent months questioning myself, feeling ashamed that our financial difficulties might be perceived as poor management," said Foskett.

Coach Dave Rennie said Jordie Barrett was the natural choice as All Blacks captain for this weekend's rematch with England at Twickenham.

Hooker and tour skipper Codie Taylor is one of four players ruled out of the game with injury, opening the door for Jordie to become the third Barrett brother to lead the All Blacks, after Scott and Beauden.

"I think anyone who would have worked with Jordie would know he's very impressive, great game understanding, both sides of the ball, he's prepared to challenge and he's been great in our leadership group."
"He's taken over the captaincy role when Codie has left the field last week and a couple of weeks ago, so, it was a pretty straightforward decision for us."
Rennie has made six changes to his starting XV, some injury enforced, with Taylor , midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown, forward Tupou Vaa'i and wing Will Jordan all unavailable.
Asafo Aumua starts at hooker, Scott Barrett and Fabian Holland are the locks with Anton Segner, Peter Lakai and Wallace Sititi in the loose forwards.

Cortez Ratima and Richie Mo'unga are at halfback and first-five respectively, while Leicester Fainga'anuku joins Jordie Barrett in the centres with Rieko Ioane and Josh Moorby on the wings. Damian McKenzie shifts from No.10 to fullback.

Richie Mo'unga will start at first-five with Damian McKenzie moving to fullback and Beauden Barrett dropping to the bench.
Rennie said once it was decided Taylor wouldn't play, the front rower wanted to let Barrett know he would be leading the team for the first time.
"I told him we were going to make Jordie captain and he said 'oh can I tell him?'. Codie was quite emotional when he passed that information on to Jordie."
Rennie said it's an "unbelievable" achievement for the Barrett family, but said he made the call to give Jordie the captaincy as he's "the right man for the job."
Rennie said Barrett's challenge will be getting the best out of everyone around him.

"He carries the team on his back. He's the one who flies out and gives you line speed and he chases things, so with the extra responsibility of captaincy, he's going to have to be really good at getting the best of others," Rennie said.
The All Blacks are determined to win at Twickenham on Sunday in the Nations Championship third place playoff and bounce back from consecutive losses to Wales and England .

The All Blacks have now lost five tests this year for just the third time in their history and they won't want to be just the second New Zealand side in history to suffer six defeats in a season. The last time that happened was in 1945.
Rennie said they were their own worst enemies in the record 37-12 defeat to the English, but he is confident they can fix the issues that plagued them last weekend.
"Our line-out's got to be better, the quality of our kicking game has got to be contestable if we're doing that," Rennie said.
"We just weren't clinical enough and made double the amount of errors that England did with half the amount of ball. And then defensively, especially set-piece, just our connection.
"We've put a lot of time into those key things and if we can get that part of the game right, then we'll be in the hunt."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2804067: Analysis - Joseph Parker's world heavyweight title fight against Daniel Dubois , dubbed "New Year's Retribution", will provide him with an excellent pay-day, not to mention a chance to win back his WBO belt.

For more than a decade Israel Adesanya was the face and force of City Kickboxing.
His success put the Morningside gym on the map as a global powerhouse in MMA.
The first man to bring gold to Aotearoa, Adesanya ignited the sport and inspired countless others to strap on some gloves.
But the former king of CKB has endured a brutal fall from the top, losing his belt, his top 10 ranking, and now his team.
The former UFC middleweight champion parted ways with his gym of 16-years back in July following his most recent defeat in the octagon.
After losing his title to Sean Strickland in Sydney in 2023, Adesanya's standing has declined rapidly. He is now riding a four-fight losing streak.
However, a new gym has brought new hope of a career resurgence for the country's most decorated mixed martial artist.
In a bid to reclaim his spot among the best middleweights in the world, 'the Last Stylebender' has moved training camps across the Harbour Bridge to Unity MMA in Rosedale.
Reflecting on the decision in a recent video on his Youtube channel, Adesanya compared leaving CKB to ending a long term relationship.
"It was a hard decision It could have been worse than a breakup but you've had bad breakups before, we all have," he said.

"Sometimes when I was younger you feel I've spent so much time with this person, I've invested so much, I don't want to lose all those years. Then you stick to it, regardless of the disrespect, the manipulation. You stick with them because you don't want those to go to waste."
Adesanya went on to say time away from the gym helped cement his decision.
"As I got older, I can see things for what they are. As hard as it was, it was also really easy once I got it done.

"I ripped the Band-Aid off. I could see the forest for the trees. It was good to get clarity. I trusted my intuition, I trusted my instincts and I trusted my judgement. I stayed away from the gym for months before I made the decision. So that way I couldn't be clouded."
However, it seems Adesanya was not just looking for a change of scenery, with evidence of a rift between him and the new UFC Light Heavyweight champion Carlos Ulberg growing stronger.
He did not elaborate on the allegations of manipulation or disrespect, however, a fan commented eluding to a possible personal feud with Ulberg.
"False accusations, I don't move like that. Someone tag Israel, that's his move."
Adesanya is set to return to the Octagon next month for the first time without CKB.

Beaten by Joe Pyfer in March in what was his second consecutive TKO and fourth loss on the trot, Adesanya is fighting to keep his career alive against the dangerous Sharaputdin Magomedov on 6 December.
Meanwhile, Ulberg continues to recover from the knee injury he suffered during his UFC light heavyweight title win over Jiri Procházka in April.
Things may get even more tense at the famed gym, with rising star Navajo Stirling now ranked third in Ulberg's division, and seriously pushing for a title shot.
The pair have maintained that a fight between them would not affect the CKB team, with Stirling telling RNZ earlier this month he has a strong relationship with Ulberg.
"I've looked up to Carlos my whole life. I know how dangerous he is. But if he's still around when I get there, I can put feelings aside. It's no biggie."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2789878: Wellington golfer Daniel Hillier is lining up some pool with his mates after he finishes what he described as "the year of my life".
2026 was a successful year for Hillier which culminated in him gaining a US PGA Tour card.
Hillier completed the World Tour season just two weeks ago in Dubai, but this week will play the first event of the new season, the Australian PGA Championship in Sydney.
The 28-year-old will then play next week's Australian Open before enjoying a well deserved Christmas break.
"Just being in New Zealand, Kiwi Summer is great," Hillier told media in Sydney.
"Go down to the beach, just switch off. A bunch of my mates who live close by, we'll have a few drinks, play pool, that's a big thing that we like to do.
"I think the biggest thing for me is just being able to switch the brain off. Being able to spend that time with friends and family is probably the biggest thing."
Hillier will have to make a few decisions over the summer before he heads to the US for his inaugural season on the PGA Tour. He said he and his wife had yet to decide where they would live in 2027.
The current New Zealand Open champion is looking forward to the new challenge of "playing on some of the greatest golf courses in the world and playing against some of the best fields in the world."
Hillier will continue to chew the ear of fellow Kiwi Ryan Fox who has been playing in the US for the last two years.
"He's (Fox) been a great sounding board, he's taken a similar path to what I have and has a few extra years of experience under his belt.
"It's great that I can bounce ideas off him and he doesn't beat around the bush as well. He'll tell you how it is and that's great, it's what you need when you're going into a new environment."
Hillier said Fox's success, including winning The Open Championship this year, has given him plenty of belief.

"I think it's great to see him do his thing. It seems like he just keeps getting better as well and thinking about the timeline of my career, I feel like I've still got a few years to try and develop my game and hone in my skills.
"It makes me feel like hopefully one day, if I keep progressing the way I am, I can end up in a similar position."
Hillier sad a long term goal is to one day play a Presidents Cup which Ryan Fox did for the first time this year.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2782897: Kiwi heavyweight boxer Joseph Parker has finally been granted his wish of another world title fight with a clash against WBO champion Daniel Dubois confirmed for 30 January.

The blockbuster fight, promoted as "New Year's Retribution", will be held at the Co-op Live arena in Manchester, England, and comes 11 years after he first held the WBO world championship belt following his dramatic victory over Andy Ruiz Junior in Auckland.

Parker and Dubois, who is still very much on the rise, were due to meet in the ring in February last year when Dubois held the IBF title but it was called off when the Englishman controversially fell ill.
The 29-year-old Dubois, who has a 24-3 record as a professional, became a two-time world champion this year after stopping Fabio Wardley in May.
Wardley was Parker's last opponent, the Englishman stopping him in the 11th round of their fight in October last year.
The formidable Dubois has beaten Wardley twice, along with former world champion Antony Joshua.
His only defeats have come against the undefeated Oleksandr Usyk (twice) and Joe Joyce.
Parker, 34, was recently cleared to fight after failing a drug test following his defeat to Wardley in London.
Parker, who has a 36-4 record, defended his WBO world title in two fights before losing to Joshua in front of a crowd of 80,000 in Cardiff in 2018.
Promoter Frank Warren said in a statement: "This heavyweight showdown will deliver a blockbuster beginning to 2027.

"It's a fight everyone wanted to see, and I'm thrilled we can now make it happen. Daniel is entering his prime and when he is on his game it is hard to picture anybody beating him. But Joseph has long promised to become world champion again, and now he gets his chance."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2780069: The Black Caps can expect pace bowler Jacob Duffy to run in with his usual vim and vigour in the second Test against India.
The 32-year-old Otago speedster would have spent the last few days recovering from a marathon effort with the ball in the drawn first Test at the Basin Reserve .
Duffy went for 201 runs as he got though 33 overs of attacking bowling.
He may have to do something similar at Hagley Oval if the Black Caps again need a bowler to bring the 'chin music'.
"He (Duffy) has shown over the years that he's a classy bowler, and he's all about the team," fellow fast bowler Matt Henry said.

"So when we suggest maybe we do a bumper plan he's not worried about his personal figures. He's trying to have impact on the game. So for him to just buy into that team-first mentality is so impressive."
"I think that's probably the quality of the side, not worrying about the outcome, but how you're trying to have impact on the game."
Henry also got through 33 overs in the Indian innings in Wellington and is expecting a similar wicket at his home ground in Christchurch.
He described Hagley Oval as "a great all-round venue," but said they will always be prepared for anything.
"I think for us the main thing is adapting. That's probably what we've put our hat on for a while now, not going in with too many preconceived ideas."
At the Basin Reserve, New Zealand recovered from 70 for five to make 368, they then spent 166 overs in the field as India scored 720 and then had to survive 120 overs with the bat to salvage a draw.

"We've obviously just been in a game which has presented some challenges, I thought we coped with a lot of them really well. You look at the way that we were able to see out that game, time in the dirt for the batters to go out there and, I suppose, find us a hard-fought draw was what was most pleasing."
India's number one bowler Jasprit Bumrah has risen to number two in the Test bowling rankings following his efforts in the first Test.
In the Test batting rankings, Rishadh Pant and Shubman Gill have risen to 6 and 7 respectively, while Glenn Phillips is up 13 places to number 17.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c38x: Disgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.
Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.
Government minister Anna Turley told LBC , external she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, while shadow culture secretary Rebecca Paul said: "This man shouldn't get a minute of airtime".

Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".
Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.
During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.
In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"
The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."

Despite that apparent combative stance, Edwards wrote on his blog on Thursday: "I want viewers to know that I did not avoid a single question, and that I answered each as honestly as I could, including those about deeply personal matters: my relationships, my temperament, my sexuality."
Explaining his reasons for giving the interviews, he said: "My difficulties became front-page news, and the account that took hold was, in places, misleading or simply untrue.
"Those promoting false narratives are also, unsurprisingly, the ones questioning my right to set the record straight.
"I was left with a choice: to let that faulty account stand forever, or to offer my own."
In a statement, Forbes said it was "an important film to make".

"It's rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues – whether it's celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment," he said.
Channel 4's documentary, titled Huw Edwards - Guilty, will be broadcast on Tuesday.
In the clip for his separate interview with the Observer and its Tortoise Investigates podcast, Edwards is seen saying: "Lots of the advice I've had is just be quiet, don't say anything."

Interviewer Ceri Thomas, a former editor of the BBC's Today programme and Panorama, said he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".
The interviews have been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.
One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday that Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn5: Veruschka was a distinctive presence on the covers of magazines like Vogue and Life in the 1960s and 70s
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.
She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary , external described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."
She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.
Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.
Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.
She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute , external .
"She worked with Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, and Valentino, but also immersed herself in avant-garde photography projects in which she painted, staged, and deconstructed her body.
"Veruschka was never just a model – she was an artist, a boundary-pusher, a rebel. Her work is considered a feminist precursor to performance art."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.
"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.
They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt , 62 , argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.
The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.
"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".
The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.
It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.
Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.
Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.
Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.
Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.
They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.
It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.
At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.
They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.
The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston.
It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.
Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.
In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.
The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.
Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.
Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjr: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.
The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.
Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".
But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.
The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.
A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts
Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app
More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters
More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate
There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.
Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".
BBC weather bulletins will now include Met Office branding (presenter Matt Taylor pictured)

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."
A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.
Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.
Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.
Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.
The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.
The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.
A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw78: The BBC said it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted"
The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.
Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."
The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".
The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".
The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".
The Department for Culture, Media and Sport told the BBC: "This government will not tolerate antisemitism. It has no place in our society.

"The BBC has a crucial role in ensuring all communities are heard and feel valued as part of our public life. That is the standard that we expect the BBC to be held to. We will consider Lord Mann's independent report carefully when we receive it."
Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019 , external , said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".
"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".
"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."
The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.
He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".
His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".
Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".
He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".
He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS , which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.
The Guardian recently reported , external that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.
"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckly: Jordan said they were taken to a sports court on the Etihad campus and were told they would not be able to leave

Some Don Toliver fans who were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live arena after an unknown substance was released have said they were "quarantined for six hours" and threatened with arrest if they did not remove all their clothing.

Jordan, 33, from Scotland, said he and his brothers were among 88 people who were taken for decontamination after the incident at the gig on Sunday night , and it "felt like I was being taken hostage".
He said they had asked for medical help at 22:15 GMT and were taken to the Etihad Stadium, where they were made to change into paper suits, and stayed until 04:45 on Monday.
"It was so traumatic," Jordan said. Greater Manchester Police declined to comment.
The force has not confirmed what the substance was and there have been no arrests.
A woman was taken to hospital, with 88 other people reporting symptoms, including coughing and chest pains.
Dry decontamination was carried out by North West Ambulance Service (NWAS), GMP said.

NWAS said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution" in line with "advice taken from national scientific advisors based on the situation".
Concertgoers said they were held for hours and asked to strip after an evacuation at Co-op Live
Jordan said his 15-year-old brother first approached police officers for help when they all started to develop symptoms 15 minutes after the incident.
"Our eyes started to feel like one sensation and then we started to feel like chest pains and coughs," he said.
"We went there for help, they obviously knew that they were keeping people there, but they never told us, 'once you're in you can't get out'.

Three hours later - at about 01:30 on Monday - Jordan said the fire service told concertgoers that they would have to remove their clothes before being taken in a van to another area of Etihad Campus.

According to NHS England guidance , external , dry decontamination - the use of a dry material to remove a contaminant - should be the "default intervention" for anyone suspected of being contaminated in a chemical incident.
The guidance also suggests patients should "remove outer clothing if affected by the substance".
Jordan said he was initially told he would not have his clothes returned for two weeks
"They said we had to strip down, clothes off, put paper overalls on and then we had to get moved into a quarantine area which was across the road," Jordan said.
Jordan claimed when he expressed concern to police officers, who were also based inside the sports hall, and asked why they needed to remove their clothes he was threatened with arrest.
"They said if I didn't commit to the decontamination, I would be arrested and charged for breach of the peace," he said.
Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service have also been approached for comment.
About 70 quarantined concertgoers were allegedly held for more than six hours before being released
In a previous statement, GMFRS said crews had been in attendance for about seven hours "to ensure the safety of every person attending the event".
GMP said 88 people were "accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed".
Jordan said that at about 04:45 an officer told them that if they gave their details they would be able to go.
Archie Grime, from Accrington, said he was sitting "doing nothing for hours" during the quarantine
"We received our clothes and shoes, but we were not allowed to put them back on, he said.
"We had to walk back to the hotel in socks and the paper gown in the freezing cold."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn4: The book is described as a "cheeky treat" filled with "charm and imagination"
A father and son have won the Waterstones Children's Book of the Year after being inspired as they enjoyed an arts and crafts evening at home.
Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son Finn, from Bristol, created Is This a Plum? after "drawing, thinking and laughing" about what some shapes look like.
Ojari said he realised that "a plum looks a lot like a hippo's bum" and it led to the pair creating a book filled with "visual tricks and rhyming reveals".

Waterstones head of books Bea Carvalho described Is This a Plum? as "picture-book perfection". She said it was "endlessly re-readable, a cheeky treat for little ones, with plenty of nostalgia appeal for grown-ups".
The playful rhyming book featuring interactive cut-outs was among 20 recommended books on the Waterstones shortlist.
The book features shapes which readers use to guess what is on the next page
Dan Ojari works at Aardman Animations and enjoys drawing with his two sons.
He said he hoped the book would make readers smile and think and, above all, "sit down and chuckle with your family and friends".
Finn has been an artist for most of his life but he said that he hoped to one day become a "real-life wizard".
He said Is It A Plum? was "very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once".
The father and son duo said they wanted to inspire children to start "drawing, writing and making things to share with the world".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr1e: The 2026 event was held in Sunderland's Herrington Country Park
BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend is heading to Brighton for 2027, it has been announced.
The annual music festival will take place in Preston Park from Friday 28 to Sunday 30 May next year.
Radio 1 Breakfast Show host Greg James told listeners he is "so excited" to bring the festival to the city as he revealed the news on air, adding: "It's going to be amazing".
Tens of thousands of fans are expected to attend the three-day event, which will feature about 70 acts, from some of the biggest names in music to new emerging artists.
Big Weekend, BBC Radio 1's flagship event, is held in a new location each year - often in towns and cities that don't get as many big live music events.

In previous years acts such as US pop star Taylor Swift came to Norwich and Swansea, grime star Stormzy performed in Exeter, pop rock band The 1975 headlined in Dundee and US singer Bruno Mars featured in Londonderry.
Breakfast host Greg said: "If Radio 1 was a place, it would be Brighton.
"It's got an amazing musical heritage, loves bringing different people together and wants to make sure fun is prioritised.
"It's actually stupid that it's taken so long for us to do a Big Weekend there. Sorry about that."
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson headlined Big Weekend this year, alongside Olivia Dean and Fatboy Slim
Earlier this year the event was held in Sunderland's Herrington Country Park, where about 100,000 music fans basked in the the sun while dancing to a host of major artists.
Grammy and Brit Awards winner Olivia Dean, Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and veteran DJ Fatboy Slim topped the bill across the weekend.
Irish star CMAT, Messy singer Lola Young, former One Directioner Niall Horan and American singer Kehlani were also on the line-up.
The vibrancy of the current electronic music scene led Radio 1 to dedicate day one of Big Weekend to its Dance Party brand for the first time.

It spanned styles, backgrounds and generations - with local lad Max Jones getting the party started on the Introducing stage, and Fisher, MK and Clementine Douglas keeping the party going throughout the day.
Big Weekend tickets are usually significantly cheaper than most major festivals, with a proportion reserved for local residents.
It has not yet been revealed when tickets will go on sale for the 2027 event and at what price.
Details about the line-up will be announced in the coming months, BBC Radio 1 said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvj6: Fashion firm Paul Smith has told the BBC it is committed to animal welfare after protesters disrupted a talk by the brand's founder in his home city.
Two supporters of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) interrupted the event hosted by Sir Paul Smith at Nottingham's Broadway Cinema on Wednesday.
The protest follows investigations by PETA into alleged animal cruelty at mohair production facilities in South Africa and Lesotho, including one it said had links to a Paul Smith supplier.
The company said it upheld the highest standards of animal welfare across its supply chain.
The animal rights group said the pair were removed from the event by security.
In a statement, Elisa Allen, PETA's vice-president of programmes, said the brand had failed to act, prompting PETA to take its message directly to the man behind the label.
PETA has called on the brand to stop using mohair in its clothing
Mohair is a fibre made from the hair of Angora goats and is commonly used in clothing.
Smith said all its mohair was certified under the Responsible Mohair Standard (RMS) and that it would take relevant action if suppliers were found to be in breach of its animal welfare standards.
A spokesperson for Paul Smith said: "At Paul Smith, we uphold the highest standards of animal welfare across our supply chain, and all our suppliers are required to adhere to these standards.
"Every batch of mohair used by Paul Smith is certified to the Responsible Mohair Standard (RMS), the internationally recognised standard for responsible mohair production.
"If there is evidence that a supplier has not upheld these standards, we will take appropriate action in line with our ethical commitments."
PETA said its investigators had filmed goats being injured during shearing, including at mohair facilities under the RMS.
Allen said: "Hundreds of fashion brands have already ditched mohair, and Paul Smith must do the right thing and follow suit.
"PETA also urges shoppers to do their part by leaving cruelty on the rack and opting for animal-free materials such as cotton, hemp and bamboo."
Other brands, such as Helmut Lang, G-Star, Gap, Fred Perry, Barbour, UNIQLO, and Zara, have already banned mohair.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjr4: TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.
Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

In a statement announcing his new role, Ramsay said he wants to bring "a fresh energy and ambition" to the show's formula of being "surprising, entertaining and [with] just the right amount of chaos".
Andrew Flintoff, Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris hosted the show before it was rested
Top Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC's biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.
They were replaced by hosts including Chris Evans and Friends star Matt LeBlanc, before Flintoff took over in 2018 with Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris.
But the show was "rested" after the former cricketer's crash in December 2022.
Flintoff was dragged face-down underneath the Morgan Super 3 car for about 50 metres. "I thought I was dead," he told a Disney+ documentary last year.
The BBC apologised and paid compensation to Flintoff following his crash.
In Wednesday's statement, Ramsay said he has had a love of cars since he grew up near the Silverstone race circuit in Northamptonshire.

"I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing," he said. "That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering.
"At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected - surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos.
"That's the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences.
"It's an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can't wait to get started!"
Former host Richard Hammond told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that Top Gear is "a grand old BBC stalwart".

"It goes back decades. We had our tenure of it and did our thing with it and went a bit crazy with it, and it'll be another incarnation of it," he said. "And great. It's a long runner, it'll carry on."
He said that he does not doubt Ramsay's credentials as a car fan, and joked that TV chefs "love three things: cooking - well in his case four - swearing, cooking, but also big watches and cars".
Hammond was seriously injured in a crash while filming the show in 2006, but said it "doesn't have to be" a dangerous show.
The BBC asked Hammond to return to the show for the new series, he said.
"They did talk to me about it. They came to me about maybe getting involved in leading the new Top Gear, and I don't want to drag it back to what it was. That's why I didn't do it," he said.
Ramsay drove in a celebrity race in Lego-themed cars at the Las Vegas Grand Prix at the weekend
Ramsay, 60, owns an extensive collection of cars including multiple Aston Martins and Ferraris, as well as a Porsche, Land Rover and McLaren Senna.
He has also appeared on Top Gear three times as a guest - in 2002, 2006 and 2017.

The BBC's director of entertainment Ed Havard said: "Gordon's fierce and fearless approach makes him a natural fit, and we're thrilled that audiences will see him in the driving seat as the show speeds into its next exciting era."
Suzy Lamb, managing director for BBC Studios Entertainment, added: "The return of Top Gear had to feel like a real TV event and Gordon fits the bill perfectly.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly: AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her

More than 800 people have complained to the media regulator about an episode of ITV reality show I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in which Mariella Frostrup accused her campmate AJ Odudu of being "aggressive".
Ofcom said 887 people had filed complaints about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.
An Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

The pair were seen clearing the air on Tuesday, with broadcaster Frostrup saying she was "sorry for calling you aggressive" and Odudu telling her it is "a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".
Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday
Relations between the pair became fractious when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode.
Tensions flared further as they and other campmates discussed their friction and the cooking arrangements the following morning.

After fellow celebrities Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney tried to smooth the strained relationship in Sunday's episode, Frostrup told Odudu she was "making a drama out of a crisis" and that she had been "thrilled there was another person" who said they could cook.
Odudu responded: "You have a funny way of showing it, that's all," before Frostrup replied: "You see, that's just aggressive and that's what keeps happening."
Odudu said she felt being called aggressive was "very harsh".
Both women later had tearful conversations with other campmates, with Odudu saying "aggressive" was "an insane word" to use about her, while Frostrup said the pressure in the camp was "too much".
They included former BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo, who said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."
Singer Beverley Knight wrote: "The word 'aggressive' feeds directly into the 'angry Black woman' trope. It IS hurtful and offensive."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."
Mariella Frostrup risked further tension when she told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well"
Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation in Tuesday's episode.

Odudu told her being called "aggressive" was "triggering because in this world, navigating it as a person who looks like me can be difficult sometimes because my experience is that my emotions and my intent are completely misconstrued".
She added: "In same way that you are allowed to express yourself, I can't express myself in the same way. We're not granted the same freedom.
"You're allowed to be emotional and passionate, and I automatically go to 'aggressive'. There's no in-between. It's like I'm 'dramatic' and 'aggressive' and that's it.
"Whereas I feel like someone like you gets to go through all the emotions of life and all of those emotions are accepted and embraced and valid."
Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "aggressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else".

"I think women who speak their mind and are forthright, that's 'aggressive', whereas a man who speaks his mind and is forthright is a 'strong man'," she said, but added that "I totally get that there's more" when race is involved.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwdd: The BBC has lodged an "urgent" appeal against a US judge's decision to allow Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.6bn) lawsuit against the corporation to go ahead.
The US president is suing the BBC for defamation over the way an episode of Panorama edited a speech he gave in January 2021, shortly before the riot at the US Capitol.
Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that the defamation case could proceed after the BBC sought to dismiss it.

The BBC has now filed an appeal with a higher court, saying there is a "complete lack of evidence" that anyone in Florida accessed the programme, and that the broadcaster made "rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary" in the US.
A BBC spokesman said: "We are surprised and disappointed by the court's decision that this case should be heard in Florida.
"As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK - and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.
"Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling."
President Trump's lawsuit accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave on 6 January 2021.
The BBC has apologised for the edit in Trump: A Second Chance, which it said had given "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".
But the corporation argued that the Panorama episode, which was broadcast in 2024, did not meet the legal criteria for defamation.
Earlier this month, federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not rule on the merits of the case.
President Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a post on Truth Social at the time.
The BBC has now lodged an appeal with the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, arguing that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.
Trump has been ordered to answer questions under oath as part of the lawsuit by 22 January.
Judge Kuntz has scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

This City Is Ours actor James Nelson-Joyce said he is "proud" of the Liverpool-based show and has defended it following criticism from the city region's mayor.
Earlier this month Steve Rotheram said he would like TV dramas set in his home city to focus on the "warmth" of the people, rather than "drugs, organised crime and criminal activity".
Nelson-Joyce, who plays Michael Kavanagh in the drama series, said: "Let's have it straight, the drama itself isn't glamourising drugs or criminality. It's showing the consequences of that."
Steve Rotheram said the crime drama was not a portrayal of the city he wanted to see

Speaking to Helen Jones on the BBC Radio Merseyside's Drive programme ahead of a ceremony at The City of Liverpool College, where a theatre has been renamed in his honour, Nelson-Joyce said: "I heard Steve Rotheram's take on this and I've kept my mouth shut but I will say something.
"Steve Rotheram's all well and good, asking for pictures and saying well done on the show, but then he tries to appease the public by saying it's not how we want to show the city.
"Let's have it straight, the drama itself isn't glamourising drugs or criminality. It's showing the consequences of that.
"If he wants to talk about it, I'm very open to contact. It's brought £9m into the city in its first season and it's done great for Liverpool, for tourism and for employment, and I'm proud of it."
BBC TV drama This City is Ours is filmed in Liverpool and Spain
