Generative AI had “zero part” in the making of the biggest video game this decade, and there’s no way it could have, experts say.
For one of the most technologically ambitious video games ever made, Grand Theft Auto VI comes with a surprisingly old-fashioned boast: it’s handmade by humans.
Generative AI had “zero part” in creating the game, Take-Two Interactive chief executive Strauss Zelnick says .
“Their worlds are handcrafted. That’s what differentiates them.”
The latest version of the hugely popular video game franchise criticised for its violent misogyny has at least one addition to draw in new female fans.
Developers Rockstar Games said the extra months "will allow us to finish the game with the level of polish you have come to expect and deserve".
How does a Kiwi street artist end up being in the hottest game of all time?

As generative AI becomes increasingly common in game development, that distinction matters to some players. New Zealand gamers told RNZ they are wary of AI-generated characters, worlds and stories. Instead, they value games where the human touch is still visible.

Auckland gamer and journalist Liam Swiggs says avid players prefer games that don't leverage AI, especially in ‘open world’ games, where players are free to explore an expansive world filled with quests and activities.
"There's a very fine line when it comes to AI being used in video games, especially open world games."
Swiggs, who reviewed the game for RNZ , reckons the difference between using AI to code and using AI to create assets is key.
"I think as time goes on - unless AI gets so good we literally can't tell a player model or an environment isn't created by a human - the use of generative AI will fade away."
"Even worse, people have been using AI to generate entire stories and dialogue [in] games, which feels even more disconnected, it's like talking to a chat bot," he says.
Long-time Wellington gamer and music tutor, 24-year-old Val Mortlock, says the growing use of AI is turning off gamers, especially Gen Z.
"I'm noticing more and more people will clock it immediately, and as soon as they realise it's AI, they don't want anything to do with it," Mortlock says.
Player Phyllis Wilton, a 24-year-old support worker from Wellington, believes that AI can’t successfully reproduce a game narrative and is unable to create real emotional reactions.
"Especially cinematic games, they rely heavily on the idea that it's kind of like a movie that you play and to have that sort of atmosphere, AI can't replicate it."
Disc 2 Games, a New Zealand-owned indie game studio, has a 'no AI policy', but producer Nadia Thorne says reaction to the use of AI tools in game development is mixed.

"You've got this ability to have this kind of huge backlash if you do use it. But on the other hand, there's also games that have been released in the last two months where the developer said that it was pretty much all generated."

Generative AI (AI that creates new content from learned patterns) game development has become increasingly popular since 2023, with AI used to generate aspects of games, or the whole thing. Half of new games on buy-and-play app Steam in October used AI, according to CNET.
Jeremy Cameron, game developer and lecturer at Massey University, believes it would be too expensive for studios to make games on a Grand Theft Auto scale using generative AI.
Rockstar Games' GTA VI artwork with character Jason and Lucia.
"Not only cost-wise, but logic-wise, it doesn't have the sort of memory capacity to make something of that scale."

As the busy Christmas season looms, Wellington foodbanks say they are under pressure with more people seeking food , and fewer donations coming in.
It follows the Salvation Army warning its foodbanks could close after government funding ends next year.
Downtown Community Ministry (DCM) supports rough sleepers, homeless people, and those most at risk of homelessness.
Director Natalia Cleland said in its last food appeal it received fewer food boxes than last year's appeal.
"That will only last us few months, it would take us through to maybe the end of February and then we'll be back to feeling desperate again for food."
October saw a rise of 89 more food parcels given out compared to October last year, a 30 percent increase.
The ministry relied on financial and food donations from the public.
"This year we had a very, very small amount of financial donations, much less, and I don't hold that against anybody, it's tight and times are tough for everyone."
The ministry said it had to spend about $4500 to top up the foodbank every month, on top of donations from the community, and community partners such as Kaibosh.
Cleland said the ministry has had discussions about whether to put limits on the number of food parcels people could access.
"My response to our senior leaders and our service delivery managers is no, I think if people are coming in and asking for food, we need to do what we can to support them.

"Let's get the message out there to the public that our foodbank and others are in high demand and we're not going to start saying no to people because it's costing us a lot of money to be able to deliver that."
Earlier this year the government budgeted $8 million in funding for foodbank distributors, with the food banks given $7m.
Minister for Social Development Louise Upston told RNZ in June the ministry would continue to monitor foodbank demand through the rest of this year, and next year.
Meanwhile, Newtown Salvation Army corps officer Andrew Wilson said supply to its foodbanks was stable.
"Supply is okay. We are always relying on the generosity of our community to support our foodbanks."
"In the last six months we've received about 500 tonnes of donated goods across the Wellington region to our foodbanks, and that demand is by no means slowing down."
The foodbank received 500,000kg worth of donated food for the Wellington region since July this year, with 4745 people who had sought assistance since then.
"We are fortunate that our community where what we receive is donations. Anything that any gaps we do find we're able to supplement with cash donations that we have."

Wilson said the Salvation Army was aware that funding has become harder to source, and it has ensured that the funding it has for its foodbanks was given evenly to those who came to the foodbanks for support.
"If our funding increased, we would easily be able to feed that same dollar value of people in a heartbeat.
"We have to be very diligent with our financial resources to ensure that the families and individuals that come to us for support are able to receive some level of food support."
The Salvation Army has a supply partnership with Woolworths. In Wellington, local Foodstuffs supermarkets such as Newtown, Island Bay, and Thorndon New World donated food to the charity.
Wilson said the Newtown branch received close to 1000 loads a week.
"We pick up bread and even some end of shelf-life meat products, which is an incredible blessing."

The new record holders say they plan to keep their title. “If someone ever beats us, we’ll beat them by another 200 feet. Every time,” Wininger said.
Upoko: Ka tākaro chess ngā hoa tata ki te tihi maunga, ka whati te rekoata
Kua whakatūria he Guinness World Record e ētahi hoa tata tokorua nō Amerika, i tā rāua tākaro chess ki te tihi o tētahi maunga i Ecuador.
I tākaro a Adam Wininger, 32 ōna tau, rāua ko Joshua Host, 44 ōna tau, ki te tihi o Chimborazo, i te rohe o Bolívar, i Ecuador, i te 31 o Māehe 2026.
E 6,277 mita (20,593 putu) te teitei o te tihi i runga ake i te mata o te moana. He nui ake tēnā i te kotahi me te hāwhe o te teitei o Aoraki, te maunga teitei rawa o Aotearoa.
Nā tēnei i riro ai i a rāua te rekoata mō te tākaro kēmu papa i te wāhi teitei rawa i runga ake i te mata o te moana.
I ngana tuatahi rāua ki te piki i te maunga i ētahi marama i mua, engari nā te kino o te huarere, kāore i taea e rāua te tae ki te tihi.
“Ko tā māua kēmu tino pai tēnei, ā, he mea mīharo rawa te tākaro ki runga i te tihi o te maunga,” te kī a Wininger ki a Guinness World Records.
I hinga i a rāua te rekoata tawhito mā te 61 mita (200 putu) pea, he rite ki te teitei o tētahi whare 20 papa.
Nā ngā tāngata nō Piritana, a Tim Maw rāua ko Neil Laughton, taua rekoata i whakatū i te tau 2024, i tā rāua tākaro i te 6,216 mita (20,393 putu) ki runga o Putha Hiunchuli, i Nepal.
E ai ki ngā kaipupuri hou o te rekoata, ka mau tonu i a rāua tō rāua taitara. “Ki te hinga tō māua rekoata i tētahi, ka hinga anō i a māua tōna mā tētahi atu 200 putu. I ia wā,” te kī a Wininger.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/pakistans: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has become the first person from Pakistan to travel into orbit, and the first astronaut from outside China to visit its Tiangong space station.
The 40-year-old blasted off on a Chinese-made rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, and docked at the space station early on Wednesday.
A space station is like a giant science lab that circles high above Earth, where astronauts live and do experiments.
Ali will stay for five to 10 days, which is much shorter than the six months Chinese astronauts usually spend there. He trained in China for months to get ready, and even learned to speak Chinese.
“I’m not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder,” Ali told reporters on Tuesday.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the trip was “the journey of 240 million Pakistanis”. That’s about how many people live in Pakistan.
The mission also matters to China, which wants to show the world that other countries can use Tiangong for research too.

China hopes to land an astronaut on the Moon by 2030. The United States aims to send people back there in 2028, for the first time since 1972. China also plans to build a research base on the Moon with Russia by 2035.
Both China and the United States say they only want to use space peacefully.
Upoko: Kua eke te kaiarorangi tuatahi o Pakistan ki te teihana ātea o Haina
Ko Muhammad Zeeshan Ali te tangata tuatahi nō Pakistan kua haere ki te ātea huri ai i te ao. Ko ia hoki te kaiarorangi tuatahi nō waho o Haina kua toro ki tana teihana ātea, ki Tiangong.

I rere atu te tāne 40 tau te pakeke i runga i tētahi tākirirangi i hangaia e Haina, mai i te Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre i te raki-mā-uru o Haina. I hono atu ia ki te teihana ātea i te atatū o te Wenerei.
He rite te teihana ātea ki tētahi taiwhanga pūtaiao nui e huri haere ana i runga noa atu i te ao. Ka noho ngā kaiarorangi ki reira, ā, ka mahi whakamātau rātou.

Ka noho a Ali ki reira mō te rima ki te 10 rā. He wā poto ake tēnā i ngā marama e ono e noho ai ngā kaiarorangi o Haina i te nuinga o te wā. He maha ngā marama i whakangungu ai ia i Haina kia rite ai ia, ā, i ako hoki ia ki te kōrero i te reo Haina.
“Ehara i te mea mōku anō tēnei rerenga. Kei runga i tōku pokohiwi te ingoa o Pakistan,” te kī a Ali ki ngā kairīpoata i te Tūrei.
I kī te Pirimia o Pakistan, a Shehbaz Sharif, ko tēnei “te haerenga o ngā tāngata 240 miriona o Pakistan”. Koinā tata te maha o ngā tāngata e noho ana ki Pakistan.
He mea nui hoki tēnei mō Haina. E hiahia ana a Haina ki te whakaatu ki te ao ka taea hoki e ētahi atu whenua te whakamahi i Tiangong mō te rangahau.

E hiahia ana a Haina kia tau tētahi o ōna kaiarorangi ki te Marama hei te tau 2030. E whai ana a Amerika kia hoki anō he tāngata ki reira hei te tau 2028, te wā tuatahi mai i te tau 1972. Kei te whakamahere hoki a Haina rāua ko Rūhia ki te hanga i tētahi pokapū rangahau ki te Marama hei te tau 2035.
E kī ana a Haina me Amerika, ko te rangimārie anake te take o ā rāua mahi ki te ātea.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/friends-p: Two best friends have set a Guinness World Record for the highest-ever game of chess played on a mountain, after climbing all the way to the summit of an Ecuadorian volcano to do it.

Americans Adam Wininger, 32, and Joshua Host, 44, set up their chess board at the top of Chimborazo, a mountain in Ecuador, at a height of 20,593 feet, which is more than 6,200 metres above sea level.
Their climb beat the previous record of 20,393 feet, which was set by two British climbers on a mountain in Nepal back in 2024, by exactly 200 feet.
The pair had actually tried to reach the summit once before, but bad weather forced them to turn back. This time, they made it all the way to the top with their chess set in hand.
“It’s our favourite game and there is something so epic about playing it on top of a mountain,” Wininger told Guinness World Records.
He joked that if anyone ever beats their record, the pair will simply climb even higher to reclaim it, by exactly 200 feet every time.
For now, the chess-loving duo can enjoy their spot in the record books, all the way up in the clouds.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/spacecraf: A European spacecraft has sent back the first close-up pictures of an asteroid that was deliberately smashed into by a NASA spacecraft, as part of a test to protect Earth one day.
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft arrived at the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system this week and released its first detailed images on 25 November 2026.

Dimorphos is a small “moonlet” asteroid that orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos. Back in 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft called DART into Dimorphos, in the first-ever test of what scientists call “planetary defence.”

The idea is simple: if a dangerous asteroid were ever heading towards Earth, could humans crash something into it to change its path and keep our planet safe? The DART test showed that it can work. The impact changed Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos by just over 30 minutes.
Now Hera’s job is to study the crater DART left behind, to help scientists understand exactly what happened and how big the effect was.
“ESA’s Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know,” said mission lead Patrick Michel.
Hera will stay at the asteroid system for months, using cameras and other instruments to learn more about how to keep Earth safe from space rocks in the future.

The Te Awa Community Library recently changed the way it serves visitors. Instead of being only a place to borrow books, it now offers homework help after school, quiet study tables, and weekly digital skills sessions. https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/black-fer: The Black Ferns will take women’s rugby to three New Zealand towns that rarely get to host international test matches, as part of their 2027 home season.

Coach Whitney Hansen’s side will play New Zealand against Canada in Nelson on 10 April, the Black Ferns’ first-ever test in the city. A week later, on 17 April, they’ll face the United States in Timaru, another first for the team.
The third home test will be against Australia in Palmerston North on 21 April, for the O’Reilly Cup. It will be the Black Ferns’ first appearance in the city since 1999.
“We’re excited to take the Black Ferns to communities that don’t often get the chance to host us,” Hansen said.
The regional tests come before a huge year for the Black Ferns, which is also expected to include the first-ever British & Irish Lions Women’s Series.
Hansen said the tour is about helping build momentum for what’s shaping up to be a special year for the team, both on and off the field.
Rugby fans in Nelson, Timaru and Palmerston North will get a rare chance to cheer on New Zealand’s top women’s rugby stars in person, without having to travel to one of the country’s bigger cities.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/christchu: A 25-year-old model and entrepreneur from Christchurch has placed fifth at the 75th Miss Universe pageant, New Zealand’s best result at the competition in more than 40 years.

Georgia Waddington represented New Zealand against contestants from 116 countries and territories at the grand final, held on 25 November 2026. She had been widely tipped by pageant experts as a frontrunner before the final.
For the national costume section of the competition, Waddington wore an outfit inspired by the Pink and White Terraces, a famous natural wonder that was destroyed when Mt Tarawera erupted in 1886.
The crown this year went to Miss Puerto Rico, Jennifer Barreto, with Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela also making the top five.

New Zealand hasn’t placed this well at Miss Universe since 1983, when Lorraine Downes became the only Kiwi to ever win the title. Since then, only a handful of New Zealand representatives have made it into the top rankings.

Before this year, New Zealand hadn’t placed in the competition since 1992, when Lisa Marie de Montalk reached the top 10. That makes Waddington’s fifth-place finish an even bigger milestone for the country.
Waddington’s result is already being celebrated back home as a proud moment for New Zealand on the world stage.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/jordie-ba: All Blacks star Jordie Barrett has been named a finalist for World Rugby’s Player of the Year award, one of rugby’s biggest individual honours.
Barrett is one of four players in the running, along with France’s Louis Bielle-Biarrey and South Africans Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche. Marx is the reigning champion, having won the award last year.
The finalists were announced on Tuesday, ahead of an awards ceremony expected later this month. If Barrett wins, he would be the first All Black to take out the award since Ardie Savea in 2023.

Fellow All Black Peter Lakai has also been nominated, for World Rugby’s Try of the Year award. His try came during New Zealand’s big 50-19 win over Australia at Eden Park in October, when the All Blacks kept hold of the Bledisloe Cup.
In the move, Barrett won a contest for a high ball, before passing to teammate Damian McKenzie, who broke through the Wallabies’ defence and set up Lakai to score.
It caps off a strong year for New Zealand rugby, with two Kiwi players now up for some of the sport’s most prestigious individual prizes.
Fans will have to wait to find out whether Barrett and Lakai can bring the awards home, with winners usually revealed once the busy November international rugby window wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/giant-new: Northland has its first wind farm, with power company Mercury officially opening the $287 million Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm near Dargaville on Monday.

The wind farm sits at Ōmāmari, on the region’s west coast, on farmland run by Pāmu. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton cut the ribbon alongside Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
“Today we recognise the skill and commitment of everyone who has helped bring Northland’s first wind farm to life,” Hamilton said.

The wind farm has 12 huge turbines, each standing 206 metres tall from the ground to the tip of the blade when it’s pointing straight up. That makes them the tallest turbines in New Zealand, and the second-tallest structures in the whole country, beaten only by Auckland’s Sky Tower.
Together, the turbines can make about 77 megawatts of electricity. That’s enough power for more than 31,000 homes once the wind farm is running at full strength.
Construction began in March last year, and Mercury says the project remains on schedule and on budget, with full power generation expected by 2027.
“We remain on track to complete the Kaiwaikawe development on schedule and on budget,” Hamilton said.
Wind farms like this one help New Zealand make electricity without burning fuels like coal or gas, which is better for the environment and for the climate.
